title: Chapter 25 — Postscript
paragraphs: In defense of the dignity of whaling, I would prefer to offer nothing but proven facts. But after marshaling his facts, an advocate who entirely suppressed a not unreasonable guess that might speak eloquently for his cause — would such an advocate not be to blame?

It is well known that at the coronation of kings and queens, even modern ones, a certain curious process of seasoning them for their duties is gone through. There is a so-called salt cellar of state, and there may be a castor of state, a ceremonial cruet. How exactly they use the salt — who knows? What I am certain of, however, is that a king's head is solemnly oiled at his coronation, just like a head of salad. Could it be, though, that they anoint it so that its interior will run well, the way one oils machinery? Much could be pondered here about the essential dignity of this royal process, because in ordinary life we think meanly and contemptuously of a fellow who oils his hair and plainly smells of it. In truth, a grown man who uses hair oil, unless for medical reasons, probably has a boggy spot in him somewhere. As a general rule, he can't amount to much taken as a whole.

But the only question to consider here is this: what kind of oil is used at coronations? It certainly can't be olive oil, or macassar oil, or castor oil, or bear's oil, or train oil, or cod-liver oil. What then can it possibly be, but sperm oil in its unprocessed, unpolluted state — the sweetest of all oils?
Think about that, you loyal Britons! We whalemen supply your kings and queens with their coronation stuff!
